content: Each year in the United States, foodborne illnesses are responsible for approximately 5,000 deaths, 325,000 hospitalizations, and 76 million cases of illness. These outbreaks often result in food recalls. October 11, 2007: ConAgra requested stores to remove its Banquet and generic brand chicken and turkey pot pies from shelves after 152 cases of salmonella poisoning were reported across 31 states, with 20 individuals hospitalized. By October 12, a full recall was issued, affecting all varieties of frozen pot pies sold under the brands Banquet, Albertson’s, Food Lion, Great Value, Hill Country Fare, Kirkwood, Kroger, Meijer, and Western Family. The recalled pot pies were packaged in 7-ounce single-serving containers marked with P-9 or Est. 1059 on the side. 2007: An outbreak of E. coli O157:H7 linked to ground beef from the Topps Meat Company in Elizabeth, New Jersey, led to the second-largest beef recall in U.S. history. 2007: Metz Fresh recalled 8,000 cartons of fresh spinach due to salmonella contamination. No illnesses were reported. 2007: Botulism was linked to cans of Castleberry's, Austex, and Kroger brand chili sauce. Castleberry Foods recalled over 25 different brands of various products with best by dates ranging from April 30, 2009, to May 22, 2009. Botulinum toxin contamination in commercially canned products is extremely rare. The CDC noted that most botulism cases historically stem from home-canned foods. 2007: An outbreak of salmonella associated with Peter Pan and Great Value peanut butter affected 425 individuals across 44 states. This was the first documented salmonella outbreak linked to peanut butter in U.S. history. 2006: An E. coli O157:H7 outbreak linked to Taco Bell in South Plainfield, New Jersey, and Long Island sickened 39 people, some of whom developed hemolytic uremic syndrome. Initially, the CDC suspected green onions as the source, but later investigations pointed to contaminated lettuce. Taco Bell removed green onions from its menu, leading to a public relations issue and a pending lawsuit. 2006: A North American E. coli O157:H7 outbreak was traced to bagged spinach packaged by Natural Selection Foods and likely supplied by Earthbound Farm in San Juan Bautista. The outbreak resulted in 3 deaths and 198 illnesses across 25 U.S. states, with one case reported in Ontario. 2003: Hepatitis A was linked to green onions in Pennsylvania. 2002: An E. coli O157:H7 outbreak associated with ground beef from ConAgra affected 19 individuals in California, Colorado, Michigan, South Dakota, Washington, and Wyoming. ConAgra recalled over 19 million pounds of ground beef, marking the third-largest recall in U.S. history. 2002: Listeria contamination in processed chicken from Pilgrim's Pride led to the largest recall in U.S. history, involving over 27 million pounds of poultry products. The outbreak caused 7 deaths, 46 illnesses, and 3 miscarriages. 2001: Salmonella contamination in unpasteurized orange juice from Sun Orchard in Arizona was traced to imported orange juice from Mexico, which had been cooled with contaminated ice. 2000: Salmonella in bean sprouts from Pacific Coast Sprout Farms caused an outbreak from Oregon to Massachusetts, sickening at least 67 people and hospitalizing 17. The contamination was linked to dry seeds imported from China and Australia. 1997: Hepatitis A was linked to frozen strawberries grown in Baja California, Mexico, and processed by Andrew & Williamson Sales Co. Thousands of students in Arizona, California, Georgia, Iowa, Michigan, and Tennessee were potentially exposed through school lunches. Six million pounds of strawberries were recalled. 1997: An E. coli O157:H7 outbreak in ground beef from Hudson Foods Company in Rogers, Arkansas, led to the second-largest recall in U.S. history, involving over 25 million pounds of ground beef. Burger King was the company's largest client. 1996: An E. coli O157:H7 outbreak was linked to unpasteurized apple juice from Odwalla. 1994: Salmonella contamination in ice cream from Schwan's Sales Enterprises in Marshall, Minnesota, sickened over 3,000 people across 41 states. The contamination occurred when raw, unpasteurized eggs were transported in a tanker truck that later carried pasteurized ice cream mix, which was not re-pasteurized after delivery. 1993: An E. coli O157:H7 outbreak from undercooked hamburgers at Jack in the Box resulted in 4 deaths and hundreds of illnesses in the Seattle area and other parts of the Pacific Northwest. 1992: Botulism was reported in New Jersey after four members of a Fort Lee family consumed contaminated whitefish purchased in Jersey City. 1985: Listeria contamination in Mexican-style soft cheese in Southern California caused 47 deaths, including 19 stillbirths and 10 infant deaths, out of 142 reported cases. 1985: Salmonella in milk from a suburban Chicago dairy caused 16,284 confirmed cases of food poisoning, with estimates of up to 200,000 cases across six Midwest states. The outbreak resulted in two confirmed deaths and was linked to 12 additional fatalities. 1985: Botulism outbreaks occurred at two White Spot restaurants in Vancouver, British Columbia, due to chopped garlic stored in soybean oil. 1983: A botulism outbreak in Peoria, Illinois, hospitalized 28 individuals, with 20 treated with antitoxin and 12 requiring ventilatory support. One death occurred. The source was sautéed onions served on patty melt sandwiches at the Skewer Inn Restaurant in Northwoods Mall. 1974: Salmonella in unpasteurized apple cider caused 200 illnesses in New Jersey. 1971: Botulism was linked to vichyssoise soup manufactured by Bon Vivant, Inc., in Newark, New Jersey. After a New York man died and his wife became seriously ill, the FDA issued a public warning and initiated a recall of 6,444 cans of soup from the same batch. Subsequent investigations revealed widespread issues with the company’s processing practices, leading to a recall of all Bon Vivant products. The company filed for bankruptcy within a month of the recall announcement.
